newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia Senate passes R&D bill with changes.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia Senate passes R&D bill with changes.

text.p: The Australian Senate, ploughing through the government's contentious budget measures on Friday, passed a bill to restrict research and development tax breaks but amended it at some cost to the budget.
The Taxation Laws Amendment Bill (No 3) also included a contentious cut to medical expenses rebates and the elimination of a small tax break for co-operatives.
Minority-party senators voted down both of those measures.
But the biggest contentious part of the bill, a drop in the tax deductability of R&D spending to 125 percent from 150 percent, survived Labor, Democrat and Greens opposition.
Government officials were unable to estimate the cost of the amendment to the R&D tax break.
The Liberal-National government wanted to exclude all syndicated claims for the tax break, but the Senate insisted that the entitlement of partnerships be preserved.
If the government had got its way in ending syndication entirely, it would have saved A$170 million in 1997/98.
So the amendment means that some fraction of A$170 million has been lost.
One government industry official doubted that the amendment would cost much at all.
The government also moved a small amendment to its own bill but, again, officials did not think thee was a significant cost involved.
The drop in the R&D deductability rate was worth $430 million in 1997/98 and an additional package of detail measures, such as tighter definitions of what constitutes R&D, was worth A$118 million.
The total value of changes to the R&D policy, then, was A$718 million to the 1997/98 budget before the amendment.
The same bill also sought to cut eligibility for a government rebate on medical expenses. The measure would have saved A$26 million in 1997/98 but the Senate killed it.

One other, very small, Senate amendment was the preservation of a small tax break for co-operatives, mostly affecting farmers. The elimination of the tax break would have saved A$2 million in 1997/98 had it survived.
